# The Sound of a Room With Someone in It

The first thing I learned at the Bureau of Unclaimed Sounds was how to open a bottle without hearing what was inside it. You held it under a thick felt cloth, turned the stopper a quarter inch, and waited for a little tug against your thumb. Then you let the stopper settle back. The tug meant there was still something in the bottle. If you didn’t feel it, you wrote EMPTY on the label and put the bottle in a crate for washing.

This was not as simple as it sounded. A bottle containing the last good laugh at a wedding might pull hard enough to bruise you. A bottle containing a man saying *I know* to his own reflection might barely pull at all. For my first three weeks, I wore a thumb splint and sent a great deal of despair to be washed.

My supervisor, Viv, said this was normal.

“In July,” she said, “we get a student.”

It was April. I understood that I was not to think of myself as temporary.

The Bureau occupied the basement of the central library, underneath the travel section. A surprising number of people came down looking for Italy. In a way, we had more of Italy than the travel section did: the bell above a bakery door in Bari, the elastic slap of wet bathing suits against a balcony in Genoa, seventeen versions of a particular whistle made by a particular grandfather in a village outside Lucca. But we couldn’t give anyone a route to Florence. We directed people back up the stairs.

What we kept were sounds that had gone astray. Most sounds finish exactly where they should. A spoon strikes a saucer; someone hears it; the matter is concluded. But a spoon can strike a saucer just as the person across the table finishes reading a letter. The sound lands a little too late. Nobody takes it in. Years later, when the café is being rewired, an electrician finds it wedged behind a baseboard.

The city distributed collection jars to its tradespeople. Plumbers brought in the best things and wanted the least credit.

One Monday a plumber named Fay brought us an onion jar with a square of masking tape on the lid. On it she had written: SECOND FLOOR, BACK BEDROOM, 18 MERCER.

“I nearly left it,” she said. “It came out when I took the radiator off. I thought it was the radiator.”

“What is it?”

“If I knew that, I’d have written it on the lid.”

She took a ginger biscuit from the tin Viv kept beside the intake forms. Fay was entitled to three biscuits per delivery, an arrangement she had negotiated herself and which we were forbidden to call a payment.

Eighteen Mercer was my father’s house. Or it had been. Six weeks earlier, after ninety minutes of signatures in a room with an artificial orchid, it had become the property of a dentist named Helen. Helen had two children and had asked whether the upstairs carpet was wool. I told her I didn’t know. Then I went home and looked up how to determine whether a carpet was wool, which involves setting a little of it on fire. I was glad I hadn’t known.

Fay ate a second biscuit and put the third in her coat pocket.

“Does he still live there?” she asked.

“No,” I said.

She nodded. She knew he had died. She was offering me a question I could answer without saying it.

By regulation, when a member of staff recognized an address, the jar had to be passed to another member of staff. I put it on Viv’s blotter. She finished peeling an orange, wiped her hands, and took down the red ledger.

“Anything you want me to know before I open it?”

“He was alone in the house for a while.”

“How long?”

“Twenty years, more or less.”

“I meant toward the end.”

“So did I.”

This was unfair to my father, who had friends and a standing Thursday lunch with a woman called Penny. It was also unfair to Penny, who had telephoned me on the morning he died and then, because I was on a train, telephoned again to tell me to get off at the right station. I had never thanked her for the second call. I had been considering staying on the train to the coast.

Viv took the jar into the listening room. I heard her chair scrape. The room was soundproof except for that particular scrape, which had got into the wall years ago and made itself heard whenever it liked.

When she came out she had written a description on a yellow card.

INTERIOR. ONE PERSON PRESENT. NO SPEECH.

“You have first claim,” she said. “If you want it.”

“I don’t remember what the rules are about family.”

“You remember all the rules about family. You typed them up last Tuesday.”

I took the yellow card. In the space marked DURATION she had written eleven seconds.

My father and I spoke on Sundays. This had not always been the arrangement. It began when I moved across town and discovered that forty minutes on a bus could, if properly managed, become a distance as insurmountable as the Atlantic. At first we called each other whenever we had something to say. Later we called on Sundays. I don’t remember who proposed this, but I remember the relief of having arrived at terms.

A typical Sunday call went like this: he told me what he had bought at the market, and I told him what I ought to buy at the market. He asked how much I had paid for something. I told him less than I had paid. Then sometimes, when we had exhausted what could be pretended about vegetables, one of us said something we had meant to keep to ourselves.

Once he told me that after my mother left, he had walked around for a year with a library book in his bag because he liked to imagine she might call and ask him to meet her somewhere, and he didn’t want to have to sit there doing nothing while he waited.

“Did you read it?” I asked.

“Twice. It wasn’t much good.”

I waited for him to tell me the title. He wanted me to ask. I knew that and still didn’t ask, for reasons I could not have explained even then. On Sundays I sometimes rationed my interest, as if I were afraid he would notice how much I had.

I put the yellow card in my pocket and left the jar on Viv’s desk.

“You can take it home,” she said.

I told her I didn’t have a place for it.

Two days later Helen came in. She found the basement without asking for Italy. She wore a long raincoat with a bright blue lining and carried a glass measuring cup in a paper bag.

“Fay says this belongs to you,” she said.

It was my father’s measuring cup, the one with the numbers rubbed off above the half-pint mark. I had left it in the bathroom on purpose. On the last morning, I’d gone from room to room with a bin bag, disposing of lightbulbs too dim to be worth keeping and socks nobody would wear again. In the bathroom I found the measuring cup by the sink. He used it to rinse his hair. I washed it, dried it inside and out, and put it back precisely where I had found it. I’d had the idea that the new family might use it for the same thing.

“Thank you,” I said.

“We would have kept it, only there are no numbers on it.”

“There are some numbers.”

“Yes,” she said. “I suppose there are.”

I could see her deciding whether to tell me something. I assumed it would be a defect in the house. I prepared to defend the drains.

“My daughter likes the back bedroom,” she said. “She says it’s the only room where she can hear the rain without seeing it.”

“Has she got the bed under the window?”

“She’s got it along the other wall.”

For twenty years I had considered that the wrong wall. I tried, briefly and with real effort, to imagine putting my childhood bed against it. Then I realized I’d already done so. My father had moved it there when I had pneumonia at nine because the window was drafty. I remembered the wardrobe on my left, where it had no business being. On the day I went back to school he moved the bed to its old position, and I had been cross with him for deciding I was well.

Helen said she ought to go. It was raining. As she reached the stairs, I asked if I could see the room sometime.

“Of course,” she said. Then she came back to the desk and took out her phone. “Would Saturday actually work? If we don’t pick a day, I’ll forget, and you’ll think I was just saying it.”

On Saturday I carried the onion jar to Mercer Street in a padded lunch bag. I hadn’t listened to it. On the bus I kept fitting my hand between the jar and the bag’s foil lining whenever we turned a corner.

Helen’s daughter was called Bea. She was twelve and not particularly pleased to meet me. Her mother had asked her to tidy the bedroom out of respect for my feelings, which from Bea’s perspective was a novel and unwelcome extension of my rights as the former occupant.

“You don’t have to show me anything,” I told her.

“I already put it all away.”

This seemed to settle the matter in favor of a tour. She showed me the desk where my father had kept his shirts and the small square on the wall where a sticker had taken off the paint. I said the sticker had been a frog. She said she liked the square better, and after a moment I found I did too.

“Do you want a minute?” Helen called from the landing.

“No,” I said, too quickly.

Bea sat down on her bed. A red charging cable trailed from beneath the pillow. There was a library book on the floor, open facedown. I could have read the title from where I stood. Instead I told them about the jar.

“Can you tell what they’re thinking?” Bea asked.

“No. Sometimes you can’t even tell what they’re doing.”

“Then how do you know it’s him?”

I said that I didn’t. This was the first time I had considered the possibility that the person in the jar was me.

I took it out of the bag. There was still a trace of onion smell around the lid. Helen asked if we should close the door, and Bea said yes, before her brother came upstairs and started making noises on purpose. Then Bea put her phone facedown on the bed, and I opened the jar.

For the first few seconds I thought Viv had made a mistake, that there was nobody present at all. There was the sound a room makes when the windows are shut and the door is open a little, a difference in the air that has no pitch but is there to be heard. A pipe ticked twice. Then somebody turned a page.

A faint roughness followed: a fingertip traveling down the edge of the paper. My father stroked the pages of books while he read. At family meals, when somebody else was telling a long story, he did it to the paper napkins. It used to drive my mother mad. I’d forgotten that. I was glad to remember it, and then, to my surprise, I was glad it had driven her mad. She had sat through a lot of long stories, with that faint noise coming from the end of the table, and sometimes a person wants to eat dinner without being asked to endure another tiny thing.

The sound ended with a bit of fabric shifting. I waited for more. I had spent eleven seconds in anticipation of the part I could tell somebody about afterward.

“Was that it?” Bea asked.

“Yes,” I said.

She picked up her phone, then set it down again.

“He must’ve been quite still.”

“He was good at that.”

What came to me then was not a scene from childhood. It was a Tuesday two summers earlier. I had been in the middle of something at work and had phoned my father because I needed to know the name of a man who had lived next door to us. He told me the name, and I said I had to go. Before I hung up I heard him say, “Oh, all right.” I had thought about that *oh* many times since his death. I’d pictured him sitting by the phone in the middle of a long day, getting up after I hung up with nowhere in particular to go. But now it seemed possible he had put down the phone and gone back to a book. Perhaps I’d interrupted him in a good part.

I put the lid on the jar. Downstairs Helen made tea. Bea came into the kitchen and asked where the measuring cup with no numbers had gone, because it poured better than the new one. I said I’d bring it back. On the bus home I kept my lunch bag on the seat beside me until a man got on with a folding shopping trolley. I put the bag on my lap and the man sat down. He smelled faintly of a swimming pool. For a while we both watched the same dog running along a fence, and when the bus got too far ahead of it he leaned forward to see if there was a gap at the other end. There was. The dog emerged at a trot, as if it had known all along where it was going.

In July we got a student. Her name was Sal and she had previously worked at an ice rink. She was better at opening bottles than I was. She could distinguish by touch between a shoe being tied and a shoelace breaking. After a fortnight, Viv entrusted her with the cupboard of disputed birds.

One afternoon a man arrived with a sample jar wrapped in a tea towel. He had found it on a high shelf while clearing out his mother’s kitchen. Her handwriting was on the label: THE SOUND OF A ROOM WITH SOMEONE IN IT.

“Can you check if there’s anything there?” he asked. “I opened it at home and couldn’t hear a thing.”

I brought out the felt cloth and loosened the lid beneath it. The tug was so slight I could easily have taken it for the pulse in my thumb. I tried a second time, holding the jar in my other hand.

“There’s something,” I said. “Would you like to use the listening room?”

He looked at the jar.

“Could somebody come in with me?”

I went with him. We sat side by side at the little table. He unwrapped the tea towel and spread it beneath the jar. It was a souvenir towel from a seaside town, printed with a map. A stain obscured part of the harbor.

When he opened the jar, we heard a woman set down a cup. There was a pause, then the small, dry click of a second cup touching the first. The man kept his hand on the lid. Neither of us moved to put it back on. Overhead, a library cart passed across the travel section and caught, as it always did, on the strip of metal between the carpet and the tile. I knew the sound well enough to tell you where it happened: just past the end of the shelf, where for years a chair had stood by a window. Sometimes somebody moved the chair to get a better look outside. Sometimes they turned it around so there would be a place for another person to sit.
